project.name: Tic-tac-toe
project.brief: Build a tic-tac-toe game in Bevy 0.20.0. Play against the computer, show the result, then play another round with a running score.

provenance.description: Selected tool actions and saved project records from the actual implementation. Routine setup is omitted. No user prompts or private session files are included.
limitations: The re-enacted terminal groups recorded tool actions; it is not a screen recording of Codex.
The game uses the same Rust rules in Bevy and in the exhaustive tests.

events.title: Build a Bevy game that can carry the whole website example

step.purpose: Build a Bevy game that can carry the whole website example
step.context: The owner replaced the proposed booking app with a video game in Bevy, suggesting tic-tac-toe. The website must show real project work rather than generic feature diagrams.
step.thought: Use one small complete game: a legal board, an opponent, a Bevy interface and a second round. Keep rules independent of rendering so game behavior can be checked exhaustively without opening a window. Record genuine roadmap changes and decisions through the existing owner; the example lives inside this repository and has its own Cargo workspace.
step.outcome: Build the game in examples/bevy-tic-tac-toe and make its actual recorded work the single website story.
step.rationale: These deliverables are easy to recognize, have real dependencies, and expose a meaningful algorithm decision without requiring private project context.
step.next_action: Create four dependent roadmap pieces and implement the rules.

events.title: Does the opponent need to search ahead?

step.purpose: Does the opponent need to search ahead?
step.context: The game needs a computer opponent. The rules are implemented and five behavior tests pass. There are only nine cells, so both a short tactical policy and a full search are practical candidates.
step.thought: A policy that takes a win, blocks a loss, then chooses the center or a corner is easy to read. It may still miss a fork, where one move creates two winning threats. Compare that candidate against every legal human reply before deciding.
step.outcome: Test the short tactical policy before choosing the opponent.
step.rationale: A concrete losing game is better evidence than assuming a familiar heuristic is sufficient.
step.next_action: Enumerate games against the tactical policy and retain the first losing sequence.
step.branch_name: How should the opponent choose a move?

Test the short tactical policy before choosing the opponent.

A concrete losing game is better evidence than assuming a familiar heuristic is sufficient.

events.title: The short policy misses a fork when it plays second

step.purpose: The short policy misses a fork when it plays second
step.context: The comparison enumerated legal human replies. The first experiment incorrectly asserted that both opening positions must have a loss; that assertion was removed so the experiment reports what it actually finds.
step.thought: The short policy has no losing path when playing X, but loses as O. The recorded move sequence shows that blocking one immediate threat is not enough against two threats. A single policy is required for both marks because the game alternates the opening player.
step.outcome: Reject the tactical policy for this game; implement full minimax search for either mark.
step.rationale: Nine cells make a complete search affordable, and exhaustive human replies can check the promised behavior directly.
step.next_action: Implement minimax with deterministic tie-breaking and enumerate every human reply for X and O.
step.branch_name: How should the opponent choose a move?

events.title: Use complete search and keep game rules outside the renderer

step.purpose: Use complete search and keep game rules outside the renderer
step.context: The tactical opponent loses when playing second. Minimax passed exhaustive human replies: 82 wins and 10 draws as X; 368 wins and 153 draws as O, with no losses. The owner specified Bevy 0.20.0.
step.thought: The opponent decision now has executable evidence. Keep Board and best_move in the engine-independent library; Bevy owns input and display. Pin Bevy exactly to 0.20.0 and check its versioned APIs before wiring the game. The browser build will run the same Rust logic.
step.outcome: Use minimax for both marks and Bevy 0.20.0 for the interface.
step.rationale: One rule implementation serves the visual game and exhaustive checks, so the demo cannot quietly test a different game.
step.next_action: Build the interactive board in Bevy 0.20.0.

[package]
name = "magistr-tic-tac-toe"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"
rust-version = "1.97.1"
publish = false

# This playable website example builds independently of Magistr.
[workspace]

[features]
default = []
game = ["dep:bevy", "dep:web-sys"]

[dependencies]
bevy = { version = "=0.20.0", optional = true, default-features = false, features = [
    "std", "default_app", "ui_bevy_render", "bevy_ui_widgets", "ui_picking",
    "bevy_winit", "default_font", "webgl2", "x11",
] }

[target.'cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")'.dependencies]
web-sys = { version = "0.3", optional = true, features = ["Window", "Document", "Element"] }

[[bin]]
name = "tic-tac-toe"
path = "src/main.rs"
required-features = ["game"]

[profile.release]
opt-level = "s"
lto = "thin"
strip = "debuginfo"

events.title: Write src/main.rs

step.purpose: Give the board a definite size before arranging the controls
step.context: The first real Bevy frame showed the last row clipped and the keyboard instructions below the canvas. The canvas itself was correctly sized at 720 by 620 pixels.
step.thought: The board used percentage width and aspect ratio inside a flex column. Its auto height did not reserve the expected space for the neighboring labels. Give both dimensions the same viewport-relative value with a 330-pixel cap, so the parent lays out the complete board and instructions.
step.outcome: Replace the board's implicit height with matching bounded width and height.
step.rationale: The board owns its square geometry. Fixing that measurement lets the parent center all the controls without offsets or hiding the clipped content.
step.next_action: Rebuild and capture desktop and compact playthroughs, waiting for each actual input result.
step.branch_name: Does the board fit at both sizes?
